**Ch 006 draft, broken pivot:**

> "The joint venture has really begun," said Tommy. "Julius P. Hersheimmer!"

In the source, the Hersheimmer line is a separate beat: Tommy and Tuppence have a short exchange about the job being "more respectable than I thought," then Tuppence asks about lunch, and *then* both of them simultaneously remember Hersheimmer. The draft compresses the skip to "The joint venture has really begun" and then immediately—attributed to the same speaker Tommy—produces "Julius P. Hersheimmer!" as if it follows from the same utterance. That is odd but parseable; a reader can infer the non-sequitur is a sudden recollection.

More damaging is what immediately follows:

> "We never told Mr. Carter about hearing from him," said Tommy.

In the source this line is Tuppence's, not Tommy's—but speaker misattribution alone is not a structural break.

Let me check for the real structural tests more carefully.

**Ch 006 — "Yes, but—you know one really has the devil of a time getting anything out of it!"**

In the source, the "it" refers to "the Government," which Tuppence introduces explicitly: *"I'm sure I don't want to be rude about the Government if you've got anything to do with it, but you know one really has the devil of a time getting anything out of it!"* The draft cuts the entire clause naming the Government: *"Yes, but—you know one really has the devil of a time getting anything out of it!"* The antecedent of "it" has been removed from the draft. The preceding exchange is only about money, with no mention of the Government. A reader cannot unambiguously resolve what "it" refers to.

This passes the gate test: a reader is genuinely confused, not merely reading a less-ornamented version. The sentence reads as though "it" refers to money itself, which contradicts the logical meaning (you can't "send in a blue form" to get money from money). The referent was deleted during compression.
